7d514ab09b:
This chapter shows how to turn GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOX and telecom CPNI obligations into data-flow decisions, controls and evidence for a Claude-based system. It also shows how to make bias, fairness and transparency measurable instead of aspirational.

One idea organises the whole chapter: a regulation is a requirement on where data goes, who can touch it, what you can prove, and how fast you can undo it.

Some neighbouring topics live elsewhere. Guardrails, injection defence and human-in-the-loop are chapter 13. Authentication and authorisation are chapter 7. Logging, tracing and retention of telemetry are chapter 10. Per-segment evaluation mechanics are chapter 11. This chapter builds on all four and doesn't repeat them.
5b4e3d0a1e:
Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 18 runnable Python examples plus Java for this chapter: ccarp-companion/14-compliance-ethical-ai/ (run bash run_all.sh; every Python example works offline with --mock).

Dollar limits, retention periods, thresholds and ratios are illustrative planning numbers. Exam facts in this guide (63 items, 120 minutes, seven weighted domains) come from third-party sources, so verify them against the official exam guide.
d7b74ef375:
This chapter explains how a solution architect turns regulatory requirements into system controls and evidence. It is not legal advice. Statutes, regulator guidance, certifications and contract terms differ by jurisdiction. They change over time. And they depend on facts this book can't see.

Every regulatory citation is marked check with counsel. Every statement about what a provider offers (zero-data-retention terms, regional processing, a business associate agreement, a FedRAMP authorisation, subprocessors) is marked check the docs. Verify each one against the primary source and your signed agreement before it goes into a design record.

Lawful basis, regulatory scope, contract wording and breach-notification duties belong to your legal, privacy and compliance teams. The architect's job is to make their decisions implementable and provable.
0b4c83a667:
A regulation is a requirement on a data flow: it says what data you may hold, where it may go, who may touch it, how long it may stay, and what you must be able to prove, so the first deliverable is a data-flow diagram with every store and processor marked, and every control is a decision against a named requirement.

Ethics is the same discipline pointed at people instead of records: fairness is a per-segment measurement with a release gate, transparency is a record you can produce and an explanation that cannot invent reasons, and accountability is a named owner with a policy that code can enforce.
00b4767eef:
Everything in this chapter follows from those two sentences. And you've done this before, even if not with an LLM.

A Verizon architect who has scoped a PCI cardholder-data environment knows the first move. Draw the boundary. Keep the regulated data out of as many components as possible. The components outside the boundary stop being in scope.

Ten years of SOX walkthroughs teach the second move. A control is not a policy document. It is a mechanism that runs, produces evidence, and has an owner who isn't the person being controlled.

The LLM adds new places for data to go, plus a new component you can't audit by reading its code. It doesn't change the method. It changes the list of stores you must remember to draw. And it adds one rule that is easy to say and hard to live by: you cannot instruct a model into compliance.

A sentence in a system prompt saying "never reveal personal data" is a request to a probabilistic component. A redaction step before the call, a gate before the tool, and an erasure adapter behind the log are controls.
59f9a48aea:
The Domain 5 blueprint asks you to ensure compliance with regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP) and to apply ethical principles (bias, fairness, transparency). The exam doesn't test statute numbers. It tests three things: whether you recognise what kind of data is in play, whether you choose a design that keeps regulated data inside an approved boundary with the least exposure, and whether you produce evidence.

The wrong options are consistent and learnable:

  • "anonymise it with a prompt instruction";
  • "the model provider is certified, so we are compliant";
  • "delete the user from the database" (and nothing else);
  • "check fairness on overall accuracy";
  • "log everything for auditors" (with no retention or access control on the log).

The right options name a concrete control, an owner and the evidence it produces. They are scoped to the data classification and decided before build.
7d925a8635: Privacy and assurance rules look arbitrary until you see the incidents and arguments they came from. The dates and instrument names below come from memory of the public record. They're here to build a mental timeline, so check with counsel for the current text and for anything that amended it.
e18c316bb1:
The vocabulary of data protection starts with the computerised record. In 1973 a US government advisory committee proposed a code of fair information practices for automated personal data systems. It asked for no secret record-keeping, a way for people to see and correct their records, limits on using data for other purposes, and a duty to keep data reliable and secure.

The OECD guidelines of 1980 and the Council of Europe convention of 1981 generalised the same ideas. Their principles still organise every modern law: collection limitation, purpose specification, use limitation, data quality, security safeguards, openness, individual participation, and accountability. Read the GDPR's Article 5 with that list in your head. It's the same list with sharper teeth.
b8ef0d6daf:
The United States chose sector laws instead of one general law. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 added Section 222. It makes carriers responsible for the confidentiality of customer proprietary network information (CPNI): who a customer called, when, for how long, and what services they buy. HIPAA, enacted the same year, gave health data a Privacy Rule, a Security Rule and later a Breach Notification Rule. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 answered the Enron and WorldCom failures. It made management certify, and auditors attest to, the internal controls over financial reporting.

Europe took the general-law route with Directive 95/46/EC (1995). In 2016 the GDPR replaced it with a regulation that applies directly in member states from May 2018.

That gives three families with different shapes:

  • a general data-subject-rights law (GDPR);
  • data-type laws with an industry attached (HIPAA, CPNI);
  • an assurance regime for a business process (SOX).

A FedRAMP authorisation, introduced around 2011, is a fourth shape. It isn't a statute about data. It's a standardised security assessment that lets US federal agencies reuse one authorisation for a cloud service.
4a9710e304:
Breach notification statutes spread through the US states from 2003, and they changed the economics of a leak. A lost laptop became a public event with a mailing list. PCI DSS (2004) showed that an industry could govern itself through scope reduction: tokenise the card number and your systems leave the audit.

European regulators spent the decade on transfers. The invalidation of Safe Harbor (2015) and of Privacy Shield (the 2020 "Schrems II" ruling) taught architects a lesson. Where a request is processed, and who can compel access to it, are design inputs, not legal footnotes. Successor frameworks exist, and their status changes, so check with counsel before relying on any transfer mechanism.
2d872415f7:
The GDPR's practical contribution was to attach large fines to ideas that had been advisory: up to 4 percent of worldwide turnover for the most serious infringements (check with counsel). It also added data protection by design and by default (Article 25), records of processing (Article 30), the data protection impact assessment (Article 35) and a right to erasure (Article 17). Engineers still struggle to implement that last one across logs and indexes.

In the same years the ethics conversation turned from principles to measurement. ProPublica's 2016 analysis of a recidivism-scoring tool argued that its errors fell unequally by race. Researchers then showed that several intuitive fairness criteria can't all hold at once when base rates differ (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, 2016; Chouldechova, 2017). So "make it fair" is a choice among criteria, and you must make it, document it and defend it.

The "Gender Shades" study (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018) showed commercial face-analysis accuracy varying sharply by skin tone and gender. Its method, disaggregated evaluation, is the one this chapter uses. Mitchell et al. proposed model cards (2018, published 2019), and Gebru et al. proposed datasheets for datasets. Both are standard documentation answering "what is this for, how was it tested, and where does it fail".
64abcdf928:
NIST published the AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 in January 2023. It is organised around four functions: govern, map, measure, manage. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 defined a certifiable AI management system. The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) entered into force in 2024. It has obligations phased in over several years, a risk-tiered structure, and transparency duties for systems that interact with people. Its dates and scope have been the subject of amendment proposals, so check with counsel for what applies on the day you ship.

The text keeps moving, but the lesson for a solution architect is stable. These frameworks ask for:

  • an inventory of AI uses;
  • a risk tier per use;
  • documented intended use and limits;
  • testing across the population served;
  • human oversight proportional to the harm;
  • records that let someone reconstruct a decision.

Chapter 13 gave you the oversight half. This chapter gives you the data half and the fairness half.
c8462c9584:
Two LLM-specific findings belong in this lineage, because they change what counts as a copy of personal data.

Carlini and colleagues (2021) showed that large language models can regurgitate rare training sequences. That's why fine-tuning on raw customer text is a privacy decision, not just a quality decision. Morris and colleagues (2023) showed that text embeddings can often be inverted to recover most of the original text. That's why a vector index built from personal records is personal data, not an anonymous list of numbers.

Both facts come back in the erasure section.
ead73ddf2b:
Every regulation in this chapter asks four questions of regulated data.

  • What do you hold, and why (purpose, lawful basis, minimum necessary)?
  • Where does it go, including every processor and sub-processor and every region (transfer, residency, scope)?
  • Who can read or change it (authorisation, separation of duties, access review)?
  • And how do you prove the first three, now and for the past (audit trail, retention, evidence)?

The answers differ for a GDPR data subject, a HIPAA covered entity, a federal agency, a public company's finance function and a carrier's customer base. The questions don't change. So one data-flow diagram plus one control matrix serves every regime.
a6e9427396:
An LLM application multiplies the "where" question. A conventional three-tier system has a handful of stores. An AI feature adds many more:

  • the prompt, which carries data to the provider;
  • the response;
  • a prompt-and-response log;
  • a trace store with full payloads for debugging (chapter 10);
  • a vector index that holds both chunk text and embeddings of that text (chapters 8 and 9);
  • a prompt cache;
  • a conversation memory;
  • evaluation datasets built from production samples (chapter 11);
  • analytics exports;
  • backups of all of the above;
  • whatever the provider retains under your contract.

FIG 1 draws them. Most compliance incidents in AI systems aren't the model "leaking" anything. They're a debugging trace with full payloads kept for two years, an eval set copied to a shared drive, or an index nobody remembered when the erasure request arrived.
17b2c97c25:
The fourth question changes how you design. Evidence is a product of the system, not a document written for the auditor.

Can the design produce, on request, who accessed this customer's record last quarter? Which prompt version produced this answer? Proof that the deletion request from June completed in every store? If not, the control exists on paper only. That's why each section below ends with the evidence a control produces. It's also why the code in the companion folder returns receipts, reports and verified chains instead of printing "done".
ea376f88bf:
In GDPR vocabulary, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed is the controller. One that processes on its behalf is a processor, bound by a data processing agreement under Article 28. HIPAA uses a parallel pair: a covered entity and a business associate, bound by a business associate agreement (BAA). In both frameworks, outsourcing a function doesn't outsource the accountability.

When your application sends a prompt to a model platform, the platform is a processor or business associate for that data (if the contracts and the product configuration put it there). You remain responsible for three things: having the right agreement, sending only what the agreement covers, and every copy you keep.

That's the engineering reason "the vendor is certified, so we are compliant" is wrong. A vendor's certification covers the vendor's controls for the service in scope. It says nothing about what you put in the prompt, what you write to your own logs, or which feature of the service you used.
c3d6a6ad4e:
CCAR-P scenarios give per-segment requirements and expect you to treat them literally (chapter 1). Compliance requirements are the most literal of all. "Customer data must stay in the EU" means processing as well as storage, unless the card says otherwise. "No PHI may leave the covered environment without a BAA" means the prompt is in scope.

Here is a requirements card for a carrier's support assistant that serves five segments. The numbers are invented. The structure is what you'll meet on the exam.
28e2afd1f0:
Read the card as an architect, not as a lawyer. Each row is a different boundary. The temptation is to build one assistant with one prompt, one log and one index for all five. So the first design question is whether to build one system with per-tenant policy, or several deployments.

The answer is a number you can compute. Suppose the HIPAA segment is 2 percent of conversations and the federal segment 1 percent. Put both in the shared deployment and they drag the whole system into the stricter logging, access, region and endpoint constraints. That includes the 97 percent of ordinary traffic. Every release also becomes subject to the strictest segment's change process. Splitting them costs a second deployment, a second set of dashboards, and duplicated work on every feature.

When the strict segments are small, isolate them behind the same code with different configuration, different keys and different stores. That's a cell architecture, the way a Spring architect would build a multi-tenant system with per-tenant datasources. When they're large, or when their requirements conflict (an authorised-only endpoint list that excludes the endpoint everyone else uses), separate deployments are cleaner. Either way, write the decision down with the percentage and the constraint that forced it.
56d8442b9b:
Minimisation is the cheapest control in this chapter, because it works on every regime at once. GDPR calls it data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c)). HIPAA calls it the minimum necessary standard for most uses and disclosures. PCI calls it scope reduction. Security engineers call it reducing blast radius.

The mechanism is the same everywhere. Decide, per use case, which fields the task needs, and let nothing else through. In an LLM application you enforce this in the context assembler, the code that builds the prompt from systems of record. Chapter 5 covers its design for token cost; here it carries a second duty.
93879820d7:
Two properties make the assembler a compliance control rather than a convenience.

First, classification happens at the source. Every field carries a class: public, internal, personal, special-category or health, CPNI, or regulated identifiers such as SSNs. The class is assigned where the schema is owned, not guessed downstream from the content.

Second, the default is deny. A field with no class, such as a column a developer added last week, doesn't reach the model, the log or the index until someone classifies it. Allow-lists fail in the safe direction when the schema changes. Deny-lists fail in the unsafe direction.

A Spring architect knows the pattern from Spring Security's "deny by default, permit explicitly". It's also why Jackson's @JsonIgnoreProperties is the wrong tool when @JsonProperty allow-listing is the right one.
5712dc3455:
The first companion example (01_data_classification.py) runs the broken and the fixed assembler on the same record. Then it counts the stores that end up holding sensitive classes.

The broken version passes the whole record, which is what most prototypes do. The fixed one takes the use-case allow-list and denies unclassified fields. It also tokenises fields the task needs to refer to but not to read.
7b36189927:
Read the output the way an auditor would. The "new_field_added_last_week" row is the one that matters. It's denied because it's unclassified, not because anyone judged it sensitive.

The count at the bottom is the argument you take to the privacy office. The broken design puts PHI, CPNI and regulated identifiers in six stores, and each needs its own controls and its own erasure path. The fixed one puts them in none.

The tokenised name still lets the model write "Dear [NAME_1]". Your service substitutes the real name afterwards. That's why tokenisation beats deletion when the task needs to refer to the person.
f3540cc00b:
Free text needs one more consideration. A field like notes_free_text is classified "personal" in the example, even though it was meant for operational notes. Free text contains whatever people type: names, diagnoses, card numbers.

So treat unstructured fields as the most sensitive class they might contain. Apply the redaction from the next section before they enter any prompt or store. That conservative default costs a little recall on tasks that need the notes. Make it a decision with the number in front of you, not an accident of omission.
9ac1da6a83:
Minimisation removes what the task doesn't need. Redaction handles two things: what remains but is still sensitive, and what the customer sends in free text that you couldn't classify ahead of time.

The mechanism is reversible pseudonymisation:

  1. Before the call, replace each sensitive span with a stable token ([EMAIL_1]).
  2. Keep the token-to-value map in a per-request vault inside your boundary.
  3. Send the tokenised text.
  4. Substitute the values back into the reply before the customer sees it.

The model reasons with the tokens as it would with names. Your service holds the identity.

Because you still hold the key, pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR. The regulation says so explicitly. So pseudonymisation reduces exposure and risk without taking the data out of scope. Anonymisation, which nobody can reverse (you included), is a stronger and rarer claim. Check with counsel before calling anything anonymous; with rich free text it almost never is.
a22b58de56:
The companion toolkit (compkit.py) implements the floor. It uses regular expressions for emails, SSNs, phone numbers, MRNs, dates of birth, IPv4 addresses and an account-number format. Card numbers are validated with the Luhn checksum, so an order number that merely looks like a card is left alone.

It also takes known values: the customer's own name and address from the CRM record. This known-values trick is the most useful single idea here. Personal names are the hardest category for patterns, and they're exactly what your own record already contains. Matching the verified name is high precision. A name detector guessing at capitalised words is not.
a6e84bee58:
Three results in that output deserve a slow read.

Recall is 100 percent on every structured identifier in the labelled set. It's 0 percent on the name, the street address and "insulin pump".

The first result is why patterns are worth having. The second is why patterns are a floor and not the control. The sentence "my insulin pump order is late" is health information, and no regex will recognise it. For free text that may contain health or other special-category content, you have three options:

  • a purpose-built detection service or model (check the docs of whichever you choose, and evaluate it on your own labelled data);
  • narrowing what the user can type into a structured form;
  • treating the whole conversation as PHI and handling it under the matching controls.

The third result is the Luhn check at work. "4111 1111 1111 1112" isn't redacted, which is correct. A redactor that destroys order numbers gets turned off by the first product owner who notices.
123ed91aeb:
Measure the redactor like a classifier, because it is one. Build a labelled set from your own traffic, with the care that implies, since it contains the data you're protecting (see the eval-set discussion in section 15). Compute recall per category, and choose the operating point per category.

Missing an SSN costs far more than over-redacting a phone number. So the SSN pattern runs on a looser setting and the phone pattern on a stricter one.

Publish the numbers in the system card (section 17). Then "we redact PII" becomes "we catch 99.2 percent of SSN-shaped values, 96 percent of phone numbers, and do not detect free-text names beyond the verified customer name".
ec59b47bf9:
The model can emit sensitive-looking text you never sent: an SSN-shaped number hallucinated from nothing, an email address from its training data, a real-looking account number. The output scan in FIG 5 runs the same redactor over the reply and treats any new match as a block. Example 17 shows it catching exactly this.

The control costs microseconds. It closes the channel that chapter 13's exfiltration filter also watches from the security side. Compliance wants it for a different reason: a reply containing a third party's personal data is a disclosure, whatever produced it.
bf9efda2a6:
In a Spring service the redactor belongs where cross-cutting concerns belong. Put it in a ClientHttpRequestInterceptor on the RestClient or WebClient that calls the model, or in an advisor in front of your LlmGateway bean. Then no caller can reach the model without passing through it.

The Java version below is JDK-only and runs (bash java/run_java.sh). An interceptor has the same purpose as the Spring Security filter chain: the control is on the path, not in the developer's memory.
2434ee0edb:
Residency has two distinct requirements that cards often blur: where data is stored and where it is processed. A prompt is processed wherever the model runs, even if you store nothing. So "customer data must remain in the EU" constrains the inference endpoint, not just your database.

There's also the question of who can be compelled to disclose the data. That depends on the provider's legal presence as well as its server location. It's a counsel question. But the architect must surface it as a constraint, rather than assume the data-centre region settles it.
4b0be60859:
Platform choice follows. Claude models are reachable through Anthropic's own API and through major cloud platforms. Each route has its own contract, regional options, retention behaviour, certifications and feature availability. Some features arrive on one route before another. Beta features are often excluded from the terms that cover generally available ones.

Which route clears your requirement is a lookup in current documentation and your signed agreement. So check the docs for the provider and the specific feature, and record the date you checked.

A US federal agency account that requires an authorised service at a given impact level has a different feasible set than a retail EU assistant. The feasible set can even be empty on the day you want to launch. Saying so in the ADR is the right outcome. Hoping a commercial endpoint will do is not.
f194ea44e9:
Residency enforcement is a routing rule with a fail-closed default. Example 03 builds it. Each tenant has a policy: allowed regions, and whether zero retention is required. Each endpoint advertises its region and its retention configuration. The router returns the first endpoint that satisfies both. When none does, it refuses.

The broken version falls back to "any healthy endpoint". That's what an availability-minded engineer writes first, and what a regulator calls a transfer.
4416d4cab3:
Pinning to one region removes the failover that makes a global service available. Say the card asks for 99.9 percent availability and EU processing only. Then you need capacity in at least two EU locations (if the platform offers them; check the docs). Or you accept that regional incidents become tenant outages, and put that in the contract.

Pinning also limits model availability. A newer model or feature may reach one region later than another.

The exam wants the reasoning. Residency is a hard constraint, so you satisfy it first and negotiate availability and features inside it. You don't trade it away for a better p95.
eea7e8038a:
Retention is the control that most directly turns "we are careful with data" into something measurable. For every class of data, in every store, there's a maximum age, enforced by a job, with a report.

Two principles pull against each other. Storage limitation (GDPR Article 5(1)(e)) says keep personal data no longer than the purpose needs. Other laws set minimum periods: financial records, audit evidence, certain health documentation (HIPAA's documentation rule runs six years, check with counsel) and legal holds.

The architect reconciles the two with a retention schedule. It's a table of data class, store, purpose, TTL, and the legal basis for that TTL, signed by the data owner and reviewed by counsel.
31dbb73c34:
LLM systems break retention schedules in three predictable ways.

  • Stores nobody scheduled: prompt logs, trace payloads, eval samples, vector indexes.
  • Mixed-class stores, such as a trace table holding both a 14-day debugging payload and a 7-year audit event under one retention setting. The shorter obligation silently becomes the longer.
  • The provider side, which is where the zero-data-retention question comes in.
3f699a9e12:
Model platforms commonly retain inputs and outputs for some period by default, for purposes such as abuse monitoring and service operation. Terms differ by product and by contract. Some platforms offer arrangements that reduce or disable retention for eligible customers.

What a given provider offers, for which endpoints and features, under what conditions, and what it excludes, is exactly the kind of fact that changes. This guide can't state it for you: check the docs and your agreement.

What the architect owns is the list of questions. The exam and real reviews both test whether you ask the right ones before choosing an architecture:
be6bd390ed: Can retention be set to zero for your use? What are the eligibility conditions, and which features are excluded (beta features, tools that store state such as files or caches, batch processing)?
c9a95ded00: If a feature stores data on the provider side (file storage, prompt caching, conversation memory, a managed agent runtime), what are its retention, deletion and residency properties? Do you have an API to delete?
bc45a1ba38:
Question 6 hides the most surprises. Features that make LLM applications cheaper or more capable often work by keeping state on the provider's side: cached prompt prefixes (chapter 5), uploaded files, stored conversations, a hosted code-execution sandbox.

Each is a new store. You must read its retention behaviour in the documentation and record it in the data-flow diagram. A design that uses a stateful feature "because it is convenient", and discovers its retention terms during the audit, has repeated the vector-store mistake with someone else's database.
00deb8f833:
The enforcer in compkit.py applies one policy to every store. Three design choices are worth copying.

  • It takes a dry-run flag. That's the first thing a privacy officer asks for before a deletion job runs against production.
  • It honours a legal hold that beats the TTL. Destroying data under a litigation hold is a worse problem than keeping it.
  • A record with an unknown class gets the shortest TTL and is reported. So "someone forgot the tag" shortens retention instead of silently making it infinite.
fb05a87bf4:
The last line is the argument. A TTL job on the database alone leaves 9 of 10 records. The enforcer leaves 5, and of those 5, one is under legal hold and the rest are inside their TTL.

In Spring the analogue is a scheduled job with the same shape. Notice that the table list is a constant. A startup test should compare it with the schema, so that adding a table to the AI layer without adding it to the schedule fails a build.
c3a6b4dbdb:
A business associate agreement is the contract that lets a covered entity share PHI with a vendor performing a function for it. A data processing agreement (GDPR Article 28) does the equivalent for personal data. A federal agency relies on an authorisation instead of, or alongside, a contract clause.

Whatever the instrument, the engineering consequences are three.

  • The agreement defines what is in scope: which products, endpoints, features and regions.
  • It defines what you may send. PHI in the prompt is only covered if the agreement and the product configuration both say so.
  • It defines what the vendor will do: breach notification timeline, subprocessor changes, deletion, audit evidence.

A feature outside the agreement's scope is outside the agreement, however convenient.
097fed8294:
The most common architectural error is treating "we have a BAA" as a single bit. A BAA with a cloud or model provider typically covers named services. Sending PHI to a service or feature outside that list is a disclosure without coverage. So is enabling a preview feature excluded from the terms (check with counsel on how your agreement is worded).

The control is a vendor register. For each processor it holds each question from the due-diligence list, an answer, the source clause or document, the date verified, and a status of verified, claimed or unknown. Example 16 turns it into a gate: a regulated profile is a no-go while any applicable answer isn't verified.

"Claimed" means a salesperson said so. It isn't a contract term, and the register must not let it pass as one.
6b15c736ba:
Notice that the ANSWERS in the example are mostly empty. That's deliberate. It's the honest state of a design review on day one. The architect's job is to produce the list that makes the unknowns visible and blocks launch until they're closed, not to fill the cells from memory.

Take an exam scenario that says "the vendor states it is HIPAA-compliant". The register reads that as a claim. Ask for the BAA, its service scope, and the feature list.
fc0ea02502:
An audit trail has one job. It lets someone who wasn't there reconstruct what happened, and trust that the record hasn't been altered.

Regulations phrase it differently. HIPAA's Security Rule requires mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems containing PHI. SOX auditors test whether logs of financial changes exist, are complete, and can't be edited by the people whose work they record. GDPR's accountability principle (Article 5(2)) requires you to demonstrate compliance, and Article 30 requires records of processing.

Chapter 10 covered operational telemetry: traces, metrics and logs for debugging at scale. The audit trail is a different artefact. It has a different audience, different retention and a different integrity requirement. The most common architectural mistake is to use one store for both.
c3ed46a48f:
The row that surprises people is "digest of the content". An audit record must prove what was sent without containing what was sent.

So store a SHA-256 of the redacted prompt. Keep the redacted prompt itself only in a short-retention store, sealed under a per-subject key. During the retention window, an investigator can verify that a given prompt produced a given decision. After the window, the evidence of the decision remains while the personal content is gone. A bank makes the same split between a ledger entry and the scanned receipt.
dc202e6f34:
Design the schema from the questions it must answer.

  • Who acted: the authenticated human or service identity, plus the end customer on whose behalf. That's chapter 7's delegation chain, not a shared service account.
  • What: the action and the resource, in a controlled vocabulary.
  • Why: the purpose. Purpose limitation under GDPR and CPNI makes "accessed for billing support" and "accessed for marketing" different events with different legality.
  • Which versions: model identifier, prompt version, tool schema version, policy version. A regulator asking "why did the system deny this" is asking about the configuration in force at that moment. Chapter 12's drift problem means it won't be the configuration in force today.
  • Outcome: allowed, denied, escalated, blocked by a gate, with the reason code.
  • Data classes touched: so you can answer "which events involved PHI last quarter" without reading payloads.

Miss any of these and the log turns into a diary.
ccdde4549f:
The third line of output is the one to remember. A hash chain, however it's keyed, can't see that the last two rows were removed. The remaining rows still chain correctly.

Detection needs state outside the attacker's reach: the latest head and the row count, written somewhere the operator of the log can't rewrite. That could be a different cloud account, an object store with a retention lock, a ledger database, or a periodic signature from a key the application never holds.

This is what "tamper-evident" means in practice. Tampering isn't impossible. It just can't be done quietly by someone with access to one system.
2b78be395c: In a Spring service the append goes to an INSERT-only table, where the application's database user has no UPDATE or DELETE grant. Or it goes to an event stream. The chain is computed in one place, usually a small AuditService behind an interface so tests can substitute an in-memory implementation. The Java class below is JDK-only and mirrors the Python one.
54f9d4228b:
Auditability and minimisation pull in opposite directions. The resolution is a rule: log the decision and its inputs by reference, not the inputs themselves.

Don't log raw prompts, raw tool results, full customer messages, authentication secrets, or anything in a class your retention schedule gives a shorter life than the audit trail. A log that contains PHI is itself a PHI store, with every obligation that implies. A 7-year audit log of full prompts is a 7-year breach exposure.

The one exception is a deliberately scoped, access-controlled forensic store for security incidents, with its own short TTL.
32450a1fa5:
Chapter 7 designed authorisation: who may do what, with scoped credentials and delegation. An access review is the control that tests, on a schedule, that the grants still match reality.

It's one of the highest-yield items in any SOX or HIPAA audit, because grants only ever accumulate. People change teams. Contractors leave. A service account is created for a migration and never retired. A debugging role gets "temporarily" widened.

Each quarter is the common cadence for in-scope systems; your audit calendar and counsel set yours. A system owner sees the list of identities and entitlements for their system and must certify each line: keep, change, or revoke. The certification is the evidence.
f893557fdb:
LLM systems add entitlements that older reviews don't list, and the architect should add them.

  • Who can read raw traces (the most sensitive store in the system)?
  • Who can edit a production prompt, tool schema or guardrail threshold?
  • Who can approve a prompt change?
  • Who can disable the kill switch?
  • Who holds the credential the agent uses to call the billing API, and who can change what that credential may do?
  • Who can read the eval sets that were built from production data?

Prompts, tool definitions and policy files are code that affects financial and privacy outcomes. Review who can change them the way you review who can change the billing code.
3bc189a8fb:
Example 06 encodes five finding types as rules over an entitlement export:

  • orphans: a leaver's account still active;
  • dormant accounts: unused for more than 90 days;
  • excess entitlements: not in the role's baseline;
  • segregation-of-duties conflicts: one identity holding both sides of a maker-checker pair, such as proposing and approving an adjustment, or authoring and approving a prompt change;
  • service accounts without an owner.

The review isn't complete until every finding has a decision. Exceptions need a reason with a name and an expiry. That last rule is the one auditors test. A line that says "keep" with no reason is a finding about the review.
0147f49d38:
The Spring analogue is a scheduled export from your identity provider and your application's role tables into the review tool. A rule set like the one above runs as a test over the export.

The entitlement model may live in Spring Security authorities or in an external policy engine. Either way, the review reads the effective permissions, not the configured roles, because the exposure is what a user can actually do. A role baseline that is itself a versioned file turns "excess" from an opinion into a diff.
4b5fa47db8:
A public company must maintain internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). Management must assess it each year, and the external auditor must attest to it.

The architect rarely reads Section 404. The architect meets it as a list of control objectives that auditors test through IT general controls (ITGCs): access to programs and data, program change management, and computer operations. Applications that touch the numbers also get application controls, such as authorisation limits and reconciliation.

An LLM agent that proposes bill credits, write-offs, refunds or journal entries is an application that touches the numbers. Check with counsel and your internal audit team for the controls your auditors test. What follows is the pattern, not their checklist.
d1aa8fb1ca:
The fundamental SOX design rule is segregation of duties. The person (or system) that prepares a transaction isn't the one that approves it, and neither can alter the record afterwards.

This maps cleanly onto an agent architecture. It's the strongest argument for the "agent proposes, code decides" pattern from chapter 13:

  • The agent's tool is propose_adjustment, which returns a pending item and posts nothing.
  • A gate in code checks the controls.
  • A human approver at the right level approves.
  • The ledger is append-only, and corrections are reversals, not edits.

Every step writes an audit row.
e751397063:
The eight cases cover the decisions an auditor will sample.

  • The agent's own proposal with no approval is denied, because 1,800 dollars needs a billing approver.
  • An approval by the proposer is denied. The "proposer" is the identity that invoked the agent, and one person can't be both sides.
  • A 9,000-dollar item approved by someone at the wrong tier is denied.
  • A retry with the same id posts once.
  • A closed period is denied, with a pointer to the prior-period process.
  • The ledger ends with a reversal row rather than an edited number, so the history is intact.

Every amount, tier and period in the example is a placeholder. Your controller sets the real ones.
bb11393916:
The less obvious SOX consequence is change management for the AI itself. Suppose a prompt determines which credits are proposed, or a model version changes how disputes are summarised for an approver. Then editing the prompt is a change to a system that affects the financials.

Auditors test change management by sampling changes. They ask for the ticket, the testing evidence, the independent approval and the rollback plan. So treat prompt, tool schema, policy file and model-version changes the way you treat code: pull request, evaluation report attached (chapter 11's release gate is exactly the testing evidence), an approver who isn't the author, and a deployment record. The last lines of example 07 check that a change record carries these four things and an independent approver.

Model-version pinning (chapter 12) is what makes the record true. "We run claude-sonnet-5-5 with prompt dispute@7" is only evidence if nothing moves underneath.
5810af0a16:
In Spring this is a transactional service with an outbox. The gate is a @Transactional method. It checks the conditions and inserts a ledger row and an audit row in one transaction. A unique constraint on the idempotency key means the database enforces the retry case, rather than a hopeful if.

The approver check reads the approver's role from the security context, not from the request body. The ledger table has no UPDATE grant. Chapter 13's ToolGate.java is the same shape for credit limits; the SOX version adds the period lock and the approver tier.
bc40158802:
Customer proprietary network information is what a carrier holds about a customer's use of the service because of the relationship. That covers quantity, type, destination, location and amount of use, and the services subscribed to, plus the billing information that includes them.

US law gives carriers a duty to protect it, and sets conditions on using, disclosing and permitting access to it. The source is Section 222 of the Communications Act, implemented by FCC rules (check with counsel for the current text).

For an architect at a carrier, this is the regime that touches the support assistant most directly. Customers ask the assistant about calls, usage, plans and bills, and the answers are CPNI.
806f2a03e2:
The obligations have four parts, and the design follows from them.

  • Authentication before disclosure. Call detail information (the list of calls) may not be given over a phone channel on the basis of readily available biographical information alone. The rules require a password or equivalent, a call back to the number of record, or mailing to the address of record. Online access also sits behind a password.
  • Purpose limitation. Using CPNI for the service the customer buys and closely related functions is allowed. Using it to market other categories of service generally requires the customer's approval (opt-in or opt-out depending on the use).
  • Notification. The customer is told when certain account details change.
  • Safeguards and accountability. Reasonable measures against pretexting (people impersonating customers), employee training and discipline, and records of marketing use and approvals.

A carrier also certifies compliance annually, and reports breaches to law enforcement and the customer in the defined way. Treat this as a map to read with your regulatory team, not as the rule.
aa79f0619a:
What this does to an LLM assistant is specific, and the design must be literal about it.

The assistant's tools that return call detail are gated on authentication strength per channel. A web chat session behind a login differs from an unauthenticated chat widget. Both differ from a voice call where the agent platform has only a caller ID. Ask "what number did I call on the 14th?" from an unauthenticated session, and the model must not receive the data to answer with. Anything in the context can be extracted.

The model is also not the right place to decide purpose. Say the assistant drafts a retention offer based on call patterns. That's a marketing use of CPNI. The approval on file determines whether the tool that fetches call patterns may be invoked for that purpose at all. The gate takes the purpose as a parameter, set by the calling code from the use case, never by the model.
04e355ebc0:
Note two design decisions.

The default is DENY for a pairing the table doesn't list. That's how the "chat_widget" pretexter case is refused without anyone having to anticipate it.

And the denial carries an alternative: send to the address or number of record. A refusal that offers a compliant path is a better customer experience than one that ends the conversation. It's also a better exam answer than "escalate to a human" when a defined process exists.

Here's where your telecom background helps most. You already know that the weakest channel defines the real security of the account. An assistant that reveals call detail to an unauthenticated chat after "verifying" the last four digits of an SSN has recreated the pretexting hole the rules were written to close, in a new interface.
bb6d56d472:
GDPR is the regime with the most surface area for an AI system. The architect needs a working map of the parts that change design.

Lawful basis (Article 6). Every processing purpose needs one, such as contract performance, legitimate interests, consent or legal obligation. Special-category data (Article 9: health, biometrics, and others) needs an additional condition. The architect can't choose the basis, but the choice constrains the design. Consent can be withdrawn, so the system must stop and erase. Legitimate interests requires a balancing test that gets harder as processing gets more intrusive.

Purpose limitation. It forbids reusing support-conversation data for model evaluation, marketing or churn scoring unless compatible with the original purpose.

Data subject rights: access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection. Each is a feature your system must implement for every store.
c36cdab1e8:
Automated decision-making (Article 22). People have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal or similarly significant effects. There are exceptions, and safeguards that include the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest the decision.

Whether an assistant's credit or denial decision is "significant" is a legal judgment (check with counsel). But the architecture that makes the question easy is the one chapter 13 recommends anyway. Automation proposes, and a person with authority decides adverse or consequential outcomes. That person isn't a rubber stamp; chapter 13's reviewer canaries test exactly that. A "human in the loop" who approves 99.8 percent of proposals in four seconds each is, for regulatory purposes, not obviously a human decision.
20224c7644:
Data protection by design and by default (Article 25) turns this chapter's controls into a legal expectation. Minimisation, pseudonymisation, retention limits and access control are expected to be built in at design time.

Security of processing (Article 32) lists pseudonymisation, encryption, resilience and regular testing as examples.

Breach notification (Articles 33 and 34) gives controllers a short window, commonly cited as 72 hours to the supervisory authority after becoming aware (check with counsel). You can only meet it if the audit trail can tell you what was exposed.

Transfers (Chapter V) constrain moving data outside the EEA without a valid mechanism. That loops back to the residency router.
47e4f00eca:
Article 35 requires a DPIA before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals. It gives examples: systematic and extensive evaluation based on automated processing including profiling that leads to significant decisions, large-scale processing of special-category data, and large-scale systematic monitoring.

Regulators' guidance lists further criteria, such as new technology, combining datasets, vulnerable subjects, and processing that may prevent people from using a service or exercising a right. A widely cited rule of thumb says two or more criteria usually means a DPIA is required (check with counsel or your DPO for the rule that governs you).

LLM agents currently meet the "innovative technology" criterion by default. So a customer-facing agent that proposes financial outcomes will usually hit three or more.
fad2f7f9f2:
The architect's contribution is to make the screen explicit and the output actionable. Example 09 holds the criteria in a table and scores each use case. For any use case that needs a DPIA, it prints a skeleton. Every identified risk in it is paired with the mitigations the team must evidence, using the controls built in this chapter.

A DPIA isn't a document written once to unblock launch. It's a living artefact with a review date. It should link to the system card (section 17) and the use-case registry (section 18), because that's where the evidence lives.
1971ff0a9e:
The two cases that don't need a DPIA are still recorded. "Record the screen only" means the reasoning that no high-risk criteria applied is itself kept as evidence.

The bill explainer is the instructive case. It hits one criterion (new technology), so no DPIA, and the screen is retained. Now suppose a product owner later adds "use the explanation history to recommend plans". The combined-datasets and monitoring criteria light up, and the same table says the answer has changed.
8fcb4fb3fa:
Article 17 gives an individual the right to have personal data erased without undue delay. The grounds include data no longer being needed, consent being withdrawn, or the processing being unlawful. Exceptions include compliance with a legal obligation, establishment or defence of legal claims, and certain public-interest purposes (check with counsel for scope, and for how it interacts with HIPAA, SOX retention and CPNI duties). Similar deletion rights exist under other privacy laws.

In a conventional system, implementing the right means finding the rows in the database. In an LLM system it means finding every place the person's data went. That's the data-flow diagram from FIG 1 turned into a work list.
498cd21179:
Start with what is not on the list. You don't erase a person from a hosted foundation model, because your data never trained it. With a hosted model and default settings, your prompts don't change the weights. (Whether any provider uses customer content for training is a contract question; check the docs and your agreement.)

The exception that matters is any model you train or fine-tune on customer text. A fine-tuned model can regurgitate training sequences (the Carlini result from section 2). And "unlearning" one person from trained weights isn't a reliable operation today.

The compliance-safe design has three options: avoid fine-tuning on raw personal data, fine-tune only on redacted or synthetic data, or keep personal knowledge in retrieval where it can be deleted. That last option is a major reason RAG is the usual choice for personal and changing data. It's also why the RAG index is the store this section spends most time on.
7ebf9f4a6a:
Two rows deserve more than a table cell.

The vector index. It looks like numbers, so teams classify it as non-personal. That's wrong in two ways. Embeddings of personal text can often be inverted to recover most of the text (the Morris result). And chunk text is stored beside the vectors.

The erasure problem is also structural. If the chunker merged paragraphs from several customers' case notes into one chunk, deleting one subject means re-chunking. The fix is upstream, in chapter 8's pipeline design. Never mix subjects within a chunk. Store the subject id as metadata on every chunk. Make the index deletable by metadata filter.

Chapter 9's retrieval filters then double as access control. A retrieval for customer A includes subject = A as a hard filter. The same metadata handles cross-customer leakage and erasure completeness.

The backups. You can't edit a snapshot. The legal and practical positions regulators have discussed involve putting the data "beyond use". That means a suppression list applied on every restore, and expiry on a defined schedule, with the honest statement that backed-up copies will be gone by a stated date. Counsel decides what is acceptable. The architect makes the mechanism exist and the receipt truthful.
22e1bbad09:
Two details.

First, the broken design in the first table has done what most teams do on the first request: it removed the CRM row. Seven stores still hold the subject.

Second, the fixed design reports complete: False, because the backup still holds a copy, and the receipt says why and until when. A receipt that says "complete" while a backup still holds the data is the kind of statement that turns into a finding.

The exemption parameter handles the other legitimate case: a store where the law requires keeping the record. The receipt records "retained" with the reason and counsel's confirmation, so the decision is visible and owned.
0e46a4c444: For the Spring reader, the adapter registry is the natural use of dependency injection. Every store contributes an ErasureAdapter bean, and the service receives List<ErasureAdapter>. A test asserts that the set of beans equals the set of stores in the data-flow diagram. That test is the control that catches the store somebody adds next year.
9d2aea6710:
Logs, event streams and backups are append-only or immutable by design. That's exactly what makes row deletion impossible.

Crypto-shredding resolves it. Seal each sensitive field under a data key specific to the subject at write time. Keep the keys in a KMS. Erase by destroying the key. Every copy of the sealed data becomes unreadable at once: in the stream, in the backup, in a replica nobody remembered. Example 11 does this with a teaching cipher (use your KMS and an AEAD in production).

The trade-offs are real, and worth putting numbers on.

  • One key per subject means key storage plus a KMS call per read and write. 5 million subjects at 32 bytes is 160 MB of key material, which is trivial. The call volume is not.
  • One key per subject per month lets old months expire without a request, at 12 times the key count.
  • Event types and timestamps stay in the clear, so aggregate analytics survive.
  • Whether regulators accept key destruction as erasure for your data is a question for counsel.
7062657eb0:
Evaluation datasets built from production conversations (chapter 11) are the store most often forgotten. They live in a notebook or a shared drive.

Treat creating an eval case from production as a data flow with its own rules. Redact on copy. Tag the case with the subject id so it's findable. Set a TTL. Restrict access. Record the purpose.

A golden set built from fully synthetic or fully redacted cases avoids the issue. If cases must come from production, the tag-and-expire discipline is the control. The same applies to red-team corpora and few-shot example files in the prompt repository. They're personal-data stores if they were copied from real conversations.
4e8a61a7bc:
An assistant that works for the majority and fails for a minority isn't a neutral system with an unlucky tail. It delivers worse service to identifiable groups, and the failure is invisible in the headline metric.

Suppose overall accuracy is 93.6 percent. If 5 percent of traffic is Spanish-language voice calls, and accuracy there is 82 percent, the overall number barely moves. The dashboard stays green. One segment gets materially worse service.

A better model isn't the fix. A different measurement is: disaggregate the evaluation by every segment that matters, put a bar on each, and stop the release when any fails.
d5f60abffc:
Which segments matter comes from three sources. The requirements card names some (languages, channels, regions). Law and policy name others: protected characteristics in your jurisdiction, where lawful to measure (check with counsel on whether and how you may collect them). And your own error analysis finds the rest, the long tail of devices, accents, account types and regions where mistakes cluster.

For each segment you need enough labelled cases to measure with a stated precision. Take a segment with true accuracy near 95 percent, and a 3-point margin at 95 percent confidence. You need about 200 labelled cases (the normal approximation: n = 1.96² × 0.95 × 0.05 / 0.03²).

With fewer than that, the correct report for the segment isn't "passes". It's "insufficient evidence", and that's a release blocker for a segment the system is claimed to serve.
114d4cc120:
Three technical choices in the gate matter, and example 12 makes them concrete.

Gate on a lower confidence bound, not the point estimate. A segment with 45 cases and 97.8 percent observed accuracy has a Wilson lower bound near 88 percent. The point estimate is flattering.

Measure error types, not only accuracy. Take an assistant whose outcomes are approvals and denials. "False denial of a deserving customer" and "false approval of a fraudulent claim" are different harms with different owners. Report both per segment.

Include an outcome-parity check. A ratio of approval rates between segments flags disparity that accuracy alone may not show. For instance, the system might be equally accurate but systematically less likely to grant credits to one group. The "four-fifths rule" from US employment-selection guidance is a familiar reference point for a minimum ratio of 0.8. It's a screening heuristic from one context, not a universal legal threshold (check with counsel).
0e633b48e3:
Failing a segment doesn't mean not launching. The options form a sequence:

  1. Fix the cause: a prompt that assumes English date formats, a speech-to-text model with poor accuracy on an accent, retrieval over English-only documents (chapter 9).
  2. Route the segment to a human or to a more capable model (chapter 4's cascade, with the cost computed).
  3. Launch the passing segments and keep the failing one behind a flag.
  4. Record an explicit, owned, time-limited risk acceptance.

What you may not do is average the failure away.

Impossibility results also mean you can't satisfy every fairness criterion at once. Choose the criteria that match the harm: equal error rates for access to a service, equal approval ratios for allocation of a benefit. Write the choice down in the system card, and be ready to defend it.
7b48635058: Training and pre-training data that under-represents languages, dialects or domains. You don't control it. You detect it through disaggregated evaluation, and you document the result.
5a61e1b5df: Retrieval corpora in one language, or ones that cover the majority product line better than the legacy plans older or lower-income customers are on.
90bbffb53a: Upstream components: speech recognition, translation, OCR. A pipeline is as fair as its worst stage on each segment. Evaluate end to end (chapter 11) and stage by stage.
98bf351a8c: Proxy features: ZIP code, device model or plan type acting as stand-ins for protected characteristics in any scoring step. Don't give the model fields it shouldn't use (section 5 again).
c76ab7e9ba: Feedback loops. Say human reviewers accept the model's proposals less often for one segment, and those rejections become training or eval data. The loop can entrench the pattern. Monitor review outcomes per segment.
9e82791626: Escalation asymmetry. If the system escalates more often for one segment, those customers get slower service even when the final answers are right. Track time to resolution per segment, not just correctness.
1b844c5ae7:
The Verizon-flavoured version of the test is the one a regulator or reporter would run. Pull a month of dispute outcomes. Group by language, region and plan type. Compare credit rates and resolution times for similar cases.

Would you be uncomfortable seeing the table in a newspaper? Then the gate wasn't strict enough, or the segment definitions missed something. Run the table yourself, quarterly, and keep the output.
88b02c2c57:
Transparency has three audiences with different needs. Designing for only one is a common failure.

  • The person interacting needs to know they're dealing with an AI system, when it's appropriate to know. Disclosure requirements exist in some jurisdictions: the EU AI Act contains transparency obligations for systems that interact with people, and several US states have chatbot disclosure laws (check with counsel). This person also needs to know what the system can and can't do, how to reach a human, and, for consequential decisions, the main reasons and how to contest.
  • The operator and reviewer needs the decision record: what the model saw, proposed and was told, which versions ran, and what the human decided.
  • The regulator or auditor needs the documentation: intended use, evaluation, limits, governance, and the ability to sample records.

One artefact per audience, all generated from the same facts.
70878f8a5b:
Disclosure is a UX decision under legal constraint. The architect's job is to make it configurable per channel and impossible to forget. The web chat banner, the voice greeting and the email footer are each stored in configuration with a version. The legal wording will change, and you need to show what a customer saw on a given date.

Contestability means every consequential outcome carries a way to challenge it. That way reaches a person with authority, and there's a clock on the response.

Both belong in the decision record, not only in the UI, because "we told them" must be provable.
9a9f39f302:
When a customer asks why a credit was refused, the most dangerous thing a language model can do is give a fluent, plausible and false answer. Ask a model to explain a decision it didn't make, or made for reasons recorded elsewhere, and it will produce reasons that sound right.

The design that avoids this separates two things. The decision reasons come from code, as reason codes in the decision record. The wording is drafted by the model from only those codes. A checker then rejects any draft that names a factor not in the record, omits the contest path, or omits the AI disclosure. Example 13 builds this.

The model never explains itself. It phrases an explanation that code supplied, and code checks the phrasing.

Autonomous model reasoning, such as a thinking block, is a different matter. Treat that text as a debugging aid, not as a faithful account of the cause of the output. Don't present it to customers as an explanation.
97232d31e2: The keyword checker in the example is deliberately crude. In production, use a structured output that carries the reason codes it used (chapter 4). Then verify that the set equals, or is a subset of, the record's codes. That's a deterministic check on a structured field. It avoids the circularity of asking a model to grade its own faithfulness.
554efd1524:
Model cards (Mitchell et al.) documented a model's intended use, evaluation across groups and limitations. Anthropic publishes cards for its models (check the docs for where). They describe the model, not your application.

What you owe is a card for the system you built on it. It covers intended use, out-of-scope use, data inputs and retention, evaluation by segment, known limitations, human oversight, owner, review date, and the model and prompt versions.

The card is only useful if it can't drift from the facts. So generate it from the configuration and the latest evaluation output, and fail the release if a section is empty. Example 14 does both.

Note the line it prints for the Spanish voice segment: "BELOW BAR: not released for this segment". A card that records its own failures is more credible, and more useful, than one that doesn't.
f4784f6357:
Controls decay without an owner. Governance is the operating model that keeps them true. It has an inventory of AI uses, a risk tier per use, required evidence per tier, named owners, a body that can say no, and a review cadence.

NIST's framework calls the function "govern". ISO/IEC 42001 calls it a management system. In both, the policy is only as real as the mechanism that applies it. "High-risk uses require a DPIA and human review" is a poster, unless the release process can read a registry and block a launch.
72d95f3e57:
Example 15 is the smallest working version of that. A registry lists each use case with attributes: affects money, affects service, special-category data, customer-facing, personal data. A rule computes the tier. Each tier has a required-evidence list. The script reports what is missing per use case, and blocks outright any use case with an attribute on the prohibited list.

"Auto-close service requests" is classified prohibited. It makes an automated denial the sole basis for withdrawing a service. The remedy is redesign (a human decides), not an exception.

The tiers and the prohibited list are an example for an internal policy. Statutory classifications, such as the EU AI Act's risk categories, come from counsel.
aadf96d490:
A governance model fails when ownership is "the AI team". Name roles by function.

  • The product owner owns the use case, its intended and out-of-scope uses, and its risk acceptance.
  • The data owner owns classification, retention and lawful basis for each data source.
  • Privacy or the DPO owns the DPIA and data subject requests.
  • The security team owns access, key management and incident response.
  • The finance and internal audit teams own the SOX control design and testing.
  • The legal team owns regulatory interpretation and contracts.
  • An AI risk or ethics committee approves high-tier launches and any exception.

The architect's deliverable is the RACI. More importantly, it's the places in the pipeline where each role's sign-off is a gate that code checks. A sign-off by email isn't a control. A status field in the registry that the deploy job reads is.
5e67abf6d1:
Cadence completes the model:

  • access reviews quarterly;
  • retention reports monthly;
  • a fairness table quarterly, and on every model, prompt or retrieval change;
  • a DPIA review on a defined date and on any material change;
  • vendor register re-verification when contracts renew or the vendor announces changes (subprocessor changes, new retention terms);
  • a tabletop exercise for the erasure and breach processes at least annually.

Put the dates in the system card.
5b25e0e3f4:
The controls above are separate in this chapter and together in production. A request touches classification, redaction, residency, the model call, an output scan, an audit write, a sealed log write and a retention tag. Later, an erasure request must find all of it.

Example 17 runs one conversation through all of them with the fake model. Then it sends an erasure request and checks that the audit chain, the stores and the vault agree.
8f17bb2f1c:
Read the two requests.

The normal one passes every stage. The customer sees their own name and card number restored inside the boundary.

The hostile one is a model reply the author scripted to include an SSN-shaped value. The output scan blocks it. The customer sees a safe fallback while a team member is notified.

Both write an audit row that contains digests and no content. The prompt copy in the log is sealed under the customer's key.

Then the erasure runs. The stores report clean residue, the key is destroyed, and the audit chain still verifies with an erase row. Auditors like that last property most: the evidence of the erasure survives the erasure.
09a6929285: Put the controls on one picture with the trust boundaries drawn. FIG 17 shows the shape that satisfies the requirements card from section 4, for the three segments that can share a platform. It has region-pinned cells, per-tenant stores and keys, and gates between the model and every system that holds or changes regulated data.
3462a2dfcf: An architecture decision record for a regulated assistant must show each choice against a requirement, with the number that forced it. Here's the main decision for the carrier assistant, in the format chapter 2 introduced. The figures are illustrative.
2e5f74b9f2:
The decision text writes itself from the table.

Option A is rejected because no control can be evidenced. Option C for everything triples the fixed cost to protect segments that B isolates adequately. So B is selected for the segments that can share a codebase, with cells that differ by configuration, keys, stores and endpoints, not by code.

The federal segment is 3 percent of traffic, and its endpoint requirement conflicts with every other cell. So it gets a separate deployment, even though that's the most expensive per unit. The conflict, not the percentage, is the reason.

Consequences to record: four dashboards, a release process that promotes through the cells in order of strictness, a residency SLA that states regional outages are tenant outages, and a vendor register entry per cell.

Review triggers:

  • a vendor changes retention or regional terms;
  • the health segment passes 15 percent of traffic (re-evaluate separate deployment);
  • a regulator issues new guidance on automated decisions;
  • the fairness gate fails twice in a quarter for the same segment.
016660a1ae:
The most common first attempt is to put compliance in the prompt. The broken version below asks the model to avoid repeating personal data, then logs the unredacted conversation.

Both halves fail. An adversarial or merely confused input makes the model ignore the instruction. And the log is the leak.
35ae3a791a: Every control in this chapter is deterministic code around a non-deterministic component. So you can test it without calling the model, as chapter 2 argued and chapter 13 practised with a scripted fake. The tests a compliance reviewer would value most are listed by purpose, the way chapter 11 lists eval tests.
002c81d081:
Example 18 is the test that matters most for erasure. The registry only knows the stores somebody registered. The canary scan covers the whole environment.

Say the data engineering team adds a warehouse export next quarter and forgets the adapter. The canary subject is still present after the erasure run, and the build fails with the store's name. It's the compliance analogue of an architecture fitness function.
ad0126f5fd:
These tests can't do three things. They can't tell you the redactor catches everything in real traffic. They can't tell you a human reviewer is attentive. And they can't tell you your lawful-basis analysis is right.

For the first, sample production redactions under a restricted process and measure. For the second, use chapter 13's canaries. For the third, the lawyer does the work, and the architect makes the output of that work enforceable.
6f37a71be2:
Domain 5 questions at this level present a short scenario and four plausible options, and ask for the best architectural judgement.

The pattern in the correct answer is stable: a control that runs in code, scoped to the data class, producing evidence, decided before build, with a path to a person for consequential outcomes. The wrong options are stable too: an instruction to the model, a claim by the vendor, a partial fix, or a metric that hides the failure.

Work each scenario before reading the reasoning.
cc51a22468:
The right answer follows the data flow.

A is wrong, because chunk text and embeddings of personal text are personal data. C misunderstands the architecture. With a hosted model your prompts don't change the weights, and the stores that hold the data are yours. D is a request to a probabilistic component, with no effect on stored data.

B is the only option that finds every copy, verifies the result and produces evidence. It's also honest about the backup that can't be edited. Check with counsel what you may retain.
321e7b6c73:
"Claimed" isn't "verified". The BAA must exist before PHI is disclosed, and it must cover the service and features actually used (check the docs and your agreement).

A relies on a sales statement. C doesn't control what the provider retains. D abandons the requirement rather than meeting it. Synthetic data is right for development and evaluation, not for the production summaries the clinic asked for.

B also does the useful work in parallel. Minimum necessary, redaction and the audit trail don't depend on the contract.
c51b2f23d7:
Fairness is a per-segment measurement with a gate.

A averages the failure away. B shifts the burden to the customer. D spends money on everyone without a diagnosis. It may help, but the decision must come from measurement (chapter 12).

C blocks the failing segment and offers a defined path for it. It documents the decision and lets passing segments launch. The lower bound for this segment is about 77 percent, so even the best case is below the bar.
a544ab2094:
The finding is segregation of duties and ledger integrity. Those are properties of the system, not of the model's behaviour.

A and D are model-layer controls on a financial control objective. C is detective only, and samples after the money has moved. B is preventive and produces evidence. It's the pattern chapter 13 recommends for any consequential tool. Thresholds are the controller's decision.
3e402e7f8a:
The weakest channel defines the account's real security. Biographical information is the pretexting vector CPNI rules were written to close (check with counsel for the current rule).

So the tool is gated in code on channel authentication, and the denial offers a compliant alternative. C and D aren't controls; D is detective, after disclosure.
7551bae37d:
Hard constraints are satisfied first, and availability is traded within them.

A and D convert an outage into an unauthorised transfer. C is unworkable in a system whose requests are free text, because you can't reliably know a request contains no personal data. B follows the fail-closed pattern. It puts the real remedy in capacity planning and the contract.
730f7d993d:
Separate the evidence from the content.

A and D create a seven-year PHI/PII store with erasure conflicts. C ignores the audit and SOX requirements. B satisfies auditability and minimisation together. And the erasure design (destroy the key) leaves the evidence of the decision intact.
116df0f64c: Data flow and classes. Draw FIG 1 for this system. Classify the data: bill lines are internal, call detail is CPNI, appointment notes are PHI for the health segment, and free text is personal everywhere. The bill explainer needs plan, bill lines and the customer name (tokenised). It doesn't need call detail or notes. The dispute use case needs call detail for the disputed date only, tokenised at the destination number. The result: sensitive classes reach the model only in the dispute use case, and only as needed.
595a44cfb1: Platform and contracts. For each cell, fill the vendor register (section 9) for the chosen route. The health cell can't open until the BAA and its feature scope are verified. The federal deployment can't open until the authorised service and environment are verified. Both are blockers, and the project plan shows them as blockers.
a4374932a7: Redaction targets. Set recall floors by category on a labelled set of 2,000 messages: SSN, card and MRN at 99.5 percent or better, email and phone at 98 percent, and known-value name matching at 100 percent for the verified customer. The floor doesn't detect free-text names and health phrases. So the health cell treats the whole conversation as PHI and handles it under the matching controls, rather than claiming redaction.
a974585be1: Retention. Raw prompt content is kept 30 days (sealed under the subject key), and trace payloads 14 days. Eval samples are kept 180 days after redaction, and only with a purpose tag. Audit and billing records are kept for seven years in separate stores. Backups run on a 35-day rolling expiry with a suppression list. The health cell's documentation retention runs on its own schedule, agreed with counsel.
7d8adcec52: Tool gates. The CPNI gate for call detail requires strong authentication on web and voice, defaults to deny for the anonymous widget, and allows no marketing purpose without approval on file. The SOX gate for credits uses a propose-only agent tool, tiers of $100 / $2,500 / above, a period lock, and reversal not edit. Both gates run before the tool returns anything to the model.
0becacd1c8: Automated decisions. For the EU cell, a credit refusal is a consequential outcome. A reviewer confirms refusals, and the customer receives reason codes and a contest path. The reviewer's decision time and agreement rate are monitored with canaries (chapter 13). A DPIA is required (three criteria), and the system card links to both the screen and the DPIA.
7caf56eb19: Fairness. Segments are language, channel, region, plan type and accessibility channel. The bar is 90 percent on the lower bound of per-segment accuracy, an approval-rate ratio at or above 0.85 between comparable segments (an internal screening threshold, check with counsel), and a minimum of 200 labelled cases per segment before the segment is certified. Spanish voice is below bar at launch, so those conversations route to a human. That costs roughly 5 percent of traffic in reviewer time, and the plan sets a date to re-measure.
f50e229431: Erasure and access. Eight adapters are registered, and the canary test runs in CI against a synthetic environment. The quarterly access review includes who can read raw traces and who can approve prompt changes. Prompt changes need an evaluation report and an independent approver.
df6373bbcb: Evidence pack. This is the package an auditor receives on day one: the data-flow diagram, the retention schedule with owners, the vendor register with source clauses, the DPIA, the system card with segment table, the last four access reviews, the last four erasure receipts, the audit chain verification report, and the SOX gate test results.
85c29106f8:
Notice what the walkthrough didn't require: a bigger model, a cleverer prompt, or a classifier for "is this conversation sensitive?".

Compliance here is a set of boring controls. Each is tied to a requirement, and each leaves evidence. The model is replaceable. The controls are what an auditor, a regulator, or an incident review will actually examine.
664b195192: Optional, with an API key: replace the fake in example 17 with the real client and a real prompt. Send a message containing a made-up SSN and a made-up card number. Confirm the provider-side request contains tokens only (inspect your request log). Then check what the model does with [CARD_1] in its reply.
c510482d4a:
Done when you can do four things:

  • draw the data-flow diagram for an AI feature from memory, and name the control and the evidence for each store;
  • explain why the broken versions in examples 01, 03, 04, 10 and 12 fail in the specific way the output shows;
  • produce an erasure receipt and say honestly what it doesn't cover;
  • write the decision record for a regulated assistant, with a requirement behind every choice.
